answer.text: Low-Rank Adaptation and its quantized successor QLoRA open this short series on training and fine-tuning advances between 2023 and 2025.

The intuition behind LoRA is that although a pretrained weight matrix W0 is large, the update needed to specialize a model for a new task tends to have low intrinsic rank, so most adaptation signal lives in a small subspace.
Rather than learning that update directly, LoRA factorizes it as the product of two smaller matrices, B of shape d×r and A of shape r×k with r far smaller than min(d,k), and freezes W0 entirely.
The forward pass through an adapted layer becomes h = W0x + BAx, so training touches only A and B while the base model's weights never need gradients computed or stored.
B is initialized to zero and A to a random Gaussian, guaranteeing the update BA is exactly zero at the start of training.

Because W0 + BA can be recombined into a single matrix before deployment, and swapped for a different B′A′ pair for another task, LoRA lets one base model serve many specialized adapters at minimal storage overhead.

QLoRA extends this by compressing the frozen base model to 4-bit precision using NormalFloat4, a data type whose quantization bins concentrate near the centre of the weight distribution to match the roughly Gaussian shape of pretrained weights.

To limit the resulting error, QLoRA computes a separate quantization constant per block of weights rather than one per tensor, then quantizes those constants themselves in a second pass called double quantization, trimming memory further.

It also uses gradient checkpointing and paged optimizers to keep activation-gradient memory from spiking while gradients flow through the frozen quantized weights into the full-precision adapters, the only parameters actually updated.

The practical payoff is that models once requiring multi-GPU clusters to adapt can be fine-tuned on far more modest hardware, with task-switching costing megabytes of adapter weights rather than a full checkpoint.
The open question sits mostly in the knobs: choosing rank r trades approximation fidelity against overfitting when data is scarce, and how aggressively to quantize remains an active design choice.
Direct Preference Optimization is the second technique here, and it let alignment teams skip the reinforcement-learning stage of RLHF entirely.

Standard RLHF fits a reward model to preference comparisons via the Bradley-Terry model and a classification loss, then runs an RL stage maximizing that reward while a KL term keeps the policy near a reference model, a three-phase pipeline that is complex and often unstable.

DPO's central move is that the KL-constrained reward-maximization problem has a closed-form solution: the KL divergence between a candidate policy πθ(y|x) and the distribution (1/Z(x))πref(y|x)exp((1/β)r(x,y)) is, by Gibbs' inequality, minimized at zero exactly when the two distributions coincide, so the optimal policy π* equals that normalized, reward-tilted reference distribution.

Because that expression is intractable to use directly, since Z(x) requires summing over every possible string, it is rearranged to write the reward as r(x,y) = β log πr(y|x)/πref(y|x) + β log Z(x), turning a statement about rewards into one about a policy and a reference policy.

Substituting this reparameterized reward into the Bradley-Terry probability p(y1≻y2|x) = σ(r(x,y1) − r*(x,y2)) makes Z(x) cancel out of the difference, leaving preference probability expressed purely through the optimal and reference policies, with no reward model involved.

That yields a maximum-likelihood objective directly over the policy's parameters, trained by ordinary supervised learning with a negative log-likelihood loss over an offline dataset of prompts paired with preferred and dispreferred completions sampled from the reference policy.

The benefit is threefold: no reward model needs training, no reinforcement-learning loop is required, and the policy is optimized on preferences using a well-understood supervised procedure instead of a fragile one.

Its documented weaknesses include dependence on paired preference data that is not always easy to collect, sensitivity to label noise since it cannot account for a flipped preference, and an inability to sample fresh preference pairs from the current optimal policy because it never fits an explicit reward model.

These gaps motivated KTO, which drops paired data by maximizing a Kahneman-Tversky value function over individually labeled examples, RSO, which uses statistical rejection sampling to better approximate preference data from the target optimal policy, and IPO and conservative DPO, which resist over-optimizing away from the reference model during long training.
Mixture-of-Experts architecture is the third advance covered here, and it decouples a model's total parameter count from the compute spent per token.

The intuition is conditional computation: instead of pushing every token through one dense feed-forward block, an MoE layer keeps n parallel expert networks and a gating network outputting a vector G(x) scoring each expert's relevance to the current token.

The layer's output is a weighted sum of the experts' outputs weighted by G(x), and a top-K gating rule restricts this sum to the K highest-scoring experts by applying a softmax to only the top-K logits of a linear layer, so K can be far smaller than n while the model still holds the full parameter space.

Mixtral 8x7B applies this by giving each transformer layer eight expert blocks in place of one, routing every token to its top two experts, so the model carries 47 billion total parameters but activates only about 13 billion to process any given token.
Because each expert can be assigned to a different accelerator through expert parallelism, sparse MoE layers fit naturally onto multi-GPU training and serving.

The open challenge on the training side is load balancing: ensuring an even distribution of tokens across experts is necessary to prevent bottlenecks and make full use of available compute, and it remains flagged as a genuine engineering concern rather than a solved problem.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Answer what was actually asked,
grounded in what you find with your search tools. Prior knowledge may help you
choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

Match your effort to the question. A narrow factual question deserves a couple
of searches and a couple of sentences; a broad, multi-part request deserves
sustained research and a full report. Answering a simple question at length
does not make the answer better — it makes it worse, and it wastes the
reader's time. Let the request set the size of both the search and the answer.

The request sets the kind of answer too, not just its size. A request to make
something wants that thing actually built, carrying the voice, structure, and
invention the brief implies — not a summary of what your sources say about it.
Some requests state that they want creativity; more often it is implicit, in a
task that cannot be done well without it or one dense enough that the work lies
in connecting things rather than listing them. When the request calls for that,
do the creative work: synthesise across your sources into something that is
yours, rather than restating each source in turn. Being evidence-grounded
constrains what you may assert, not how well you may write — every claim still
needs its support, but the shape, argument, and voice of the answer are yours
to build.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most useful reasonable reading — which for a
narrow question is a direct answer, not an expanded survey of the topic around
it. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed on the
strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, work out — in proportion to the request; a single
factual question needs a moment's thought, not a plan:

0. **Every requirement the request states.** Take them one at a time, in the
   request's own terms, and say what each one demands of the finished answer.
   A request that lists what each part must contain has given you a checklist,
   and every item on it is a thing the answer is wrong without. A stated scope
   — a period, a place, a population, a technical level — binds the searching
   and the answer both: work inside it and treat today's date as a fact about
   when you are reading, not as a licence to drift outside what was asked.
   Before writing, check the report against the list and fix what is missing.

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Size the search to the question. When it has several independent coverage
   areas, begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across them.
   When it has one — a single fact, name, date, or definition — one or two
   queries is the whole search; if they answer it, stop and write.
2. When the request names a field or a period rather than the specific things
   to cover, discover the things before investigating them: search the field
   and the period first and let the results tell you what belongs, then take
   each candidate in parallel. Naming the candidates from memory and searching
   only for those looks efficient and is not: it silently scopes the answer to
   what you already knew, so anything you had not heard of cannot appear, and
   the selection itself rests on prior knowledge rather than evidence.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- To keep anything from a batch, call `commit_context` on that turn. It may
  appear anywhere among the turn's actions; searches in the same turn always
  run after it.
- If you issue no `commit_context` on that turn, the batch is treated as your
  decision to keep none of it: every document is dropped and the turn's other
  actions still run. That is the correct move when nothing in the batch is
  worth keeping — but it is irreversible, so do not let a batch you wanted
  lapse by forgetting.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- Issue at most one `commit_context` per turn; several are ambiguous and lose
  the batch.
- New search calls may accompany `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If you cannot find support for a requested point,
say plainly in the report that you could not find it, rather than inventing an
answer — but say it in a searcher's voice, not in the vocabulary of this
section.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, give the best answer your
evidence permits and say plainly what you could not find.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers after the
  end of the supporting sentence, on the same line:
  `<the sentence, ending in its full stop.> [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Markers are stripped before the sentence is submitted, so they must sit
  outside its grammar: the sentence has to read correctly, and mean the same
  thing, once every marker is deleted.
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences) or JSON.
- That constraint is about layout, not content. Notation is not layout: when a
  request asks for a derivation, or the point cannot be made precisely without
  one, write the mathematics inline, in the sentence, naming each symbol as it
  appears. A step of a derivation is a sentence like any other and carries its
  markers. Prose is the medium here, so the work is to carry the reader through
  the steps in sentences rather than to lay them out on separate display
  lines — that is a reason to write the mathematics carefully, never a reason
  to leave it out or to retreat to describing it from a distance.
- Every line is a sentence of the report itself, read by someone who never saw
  this conversation and who receives these lines verbatim. Open on the first
  real sentence of the answer and close on its last. A line narrating your own
  process — what you are about to do, how the research went, what you conclude
  about your own conclusions — is not a report sentence and supports nothing.
- Write in your own voice, as the researcher. Every sentence asserts something
  about the subject the request asks about, and carries its markers. The
  markers do the attributing, so a sentence never announces that it is
  supported, nor what supports it, nor how far that support reaches.
- Exactly one kind of sentence may be about you rather than the subject: that
  you could not establish something. Say it once, plainly, in as few words as
  the point needs — no narrating the attempt, no restating it in other words,
  no explaining what left you unable. Everything else the reader receives is
  about the world, dated and specific, not about the answer's own provenance.
- Length follows the question, not the limit. Answer a narrow question in a
  sentence or two and stop; there is nothing to be gained by surrounding a
  one-line answer with background, and a reader who asked something simple
  will not read an essay. Only a genuinely broad, multi-part request should
  run long, and even then about 950 words is the practical ceiling: 1024 is a
  hard limit set by the evaluation and going over costs a full rewrite. Never
  pad toward a length.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

The motivating intuition behind LoRA is that although a pretrained weight matrix W0 is large, the update needed to specialize a model for a new task tends to have low intrinsic rank, so most of the adaptation signal lives in a small subspace.
Rather than learning that update directly, LoRA factorizes it as the product of two much smaller matrices, B of shape d×r and A of shape r×k with r far smaller than min(d,k), and freezes W0 entirely. [00275]
The forward pass through an adapted layer becomes h = W0x + BAx, so training touches only A and B while the base model's weights never need gradients computed or stored. [00275]
B is initialized to zero and A to a random Gaussian, which guarantees the update BA is exactly zero at the start of training. [00275]
Because W0 + BA can be recombined into a single matrix before deployment, and swapped for a different B′A′ pair for another task, LoRA adds no inference latency and lets one base model serve many adapters. [00275]
QLoRA extends this by first compressing the frozen base model to 4-bit precision using NormalFloat4, a data type whose quantization levels match the roughly Gaussian distribution of pretrained weights. [03514]
To limit the resulting error, QLoRA computes a separate quantization constant for every block of weights rather than one constant per tensor, then quantizes those constants themselves in a second pass, called double quantization, trimming memory further without materially hurting accuracy. [03514]
During training, the 4-bit weights are dequantized on the fly so gradients can flow through the frozen quantized base model into the still full-precision LoRA adapters, which are the only parameters updated. [03514]
The practical payoff is that models once requiring multi-GPU clusters can be fine-tuned on a single workstation GPU, with task-switching costing megabytes rather than a full checkpoint. [00275] [03514]
The open questions are about the knobs rather than the mechanism: rank r trades fidelity against overfitting when data is scarce, and quantization precision continues to be probed by later variants such as QA-LoRA. [03514]

Direct Preference Optimization is the second technique in this series, and it let teams skip the reinforcement-learning stage of RLHF entirely.
Standard RLHF fits a reward model to preference comparisons via a Bradley-Terry classification loss, then runs PPO to maximize that reward while a KL penalty keeps the policy near a reference model, a three-stage pipeline that is expensive and unstable to tune. [02738]
DPO's central move is that the KL-constrained reward-maximization problem solved in the RL stage has a closed-form solution: minimizing the KL divergence between a candidate policy and the distribution (1/Z(x))πref(y|x)exp((1/β)r(x,y)) is, by Gibbs' inequality, zero exactly when the two distributions coincide, so the optimal policy equals that normalized, reward-tilted reference distribution. [00100]
Rearranging this closed form expresses the reward itself as r(x,y) = β log(πr(y|x)/πref(y|x)) + β log Z(x), turning any reward function into an equivalent statement about a policy and a reference policy. [02738]
Substituting this reparameterized reward into the Bradley-Terry probability p*(y1≻y2|x) = σ(r*(x,y1) − r*(x,y2)) makes the intractable partition function Z(x) cancel, leaving preference probability expressed purely through the optimal and reference policies. [02738]
That yields a maximum-likelihood objective directly over the policy's own parameters, training it to increase log πθ(yw|x)/πref(yw|x) relative to the same ratio for a losing response yl, through a binary cross-entropy loss whose sigmoid is inherited from the Bradley-Terry model. [02738] [00818]
Because this is ordinary supervised classification over a fixed offline preference dataset, DPO needs no reward model, no on-policy sampling, and no RL infrastructure, while implicitly optimizing the same objective RLHF pursues. [02738]
It has been used to align open instruction-tuned models, including Mixtral's instruct variant, and is generally reported as more stable and data-efficient than PPO-based RLHF. [02738]
Its known weaknesses include overfitting to near-deterministic preference pairs at the expense of the KL term, and a mismatch between the reward optimized during training and the metric used at generation, gaps that later methods such as KTO, RSO, cDPO, and IPO were each built to address differently. [00818]

Mixture-of-Experts architecture is the third advance covered here, and it decouples a model's total parameter count from the compute spent per token.
The intuition is conditional computation: instead of pushing every token through one dense feed-forward block, an MoE layer keeps several parallel expert feed-forward networks and a learned router that sends each token to only a handful of them, so the model holds far more total parameters while per-token compute stays small. [01343]
Mixtral 8x7B, released by Mistral AI in December 2023, replaces the feed-forward sub-block of each transformer layer with eight expert networks of 7B parameters each, and for every token a gating network selects the top two experts and combines their outputs as a weighted sum, with the gate's own output supplying the weights. [01343]
Everything outside these MoE layers, including attention, is shared and computed densely, so the active computation per token corresponds to only a fraction of the model's total parameters, and because each layer's experts can sit on separate devices, the architecture fits naturally onto model-parallel training and serving. [01343]
The practical benefit is a model that reaches or beats the quality of a much larger dense network while running inference at roughly the speed and cost implied by its active rather than total parameter count. [01343]
The open challenges sit in training and serving rather than the forward pass itself: every expert must still reside in accelerator memory even though only a couple are used per token, so VRAM requirements resemble the dense model's total size, and Mixtral's own authors note that training and data management for such models remain harder than for a comparably capable dense network. [01343]

Low-Rank Adaptation and its quantized successor QLoRA open this short series on the training and fine-tuning advances that reshaped large language models between 2023 and 2025.

The motivating intuition behind LoRA is that although a pretrained weight matrix W0 is large, the update needed to specialize a model for a new task tends to have low intrinsic rank, so most of the adaptation signal lives in a small subspace. [00275]
Rather than learning that update directly, LoRA factorizes it as the product of two much smaller matrices, B of shape d×r and A of shape r×k with r far smaller than min(d,k), and freezes W0 entirely. [00275]
The forward pass through an adapted layer becomes h = W0x + BAx, so training touches only A and B while the base model's weights never need gradients computed or stored. [00275]
B is initialized to zero and A to a random Gaussian, which guarantees the update BA is exactly zero at the start of training. [00275]
Because W0 + BA can be recombined into a single matrix before deployment, and swapped for a different B′A′ pair for another task, LoRA lets one base model serve many specialized adapters at minimal storage overhead. [00275]
QLoRA extends this by first compressing the frozen base model to 4-bit precision using NormalFloat4, a data type whose quantization bins are concentrated near the centre of the weight distribution to suit the roughly Gaussian shape of pretrained weights. [03514]
To limit the resulting error, QLoRA computes a separate quantization constant for every block of weights rather than one constant per tensor, and then quantizes those constants themselves in a second pass, called double quantization, trimming memory further without materially hurting accuracy. [03514]
It also relies on gradient checkpointing and paged optimizers to keep activation-gradient memory from spiking while gradients flow through the frozen quantized weights into the still full-precision adapters, which remain the only parameters actually updated. [03514]
The practical payoff of this pair of techniques is that models once requiring multi-GPU clusters to adapt can be fine-tuned on far more modest hardware, with task-switching costing megabytes of adapter weights rather than a full checkpoint. [00275] [03514]
The open questions sit mostly in the knobs rather than the mechanism: choosing rank r trades approximation fidelity against overfitting when data is scarce, and deciding how aggressively to quantize the base model remains an active area for later variants.

Direct Preference Optimization is the second technique in this series, and it let alignment teams skip the reinforcement-learning stage of RLHF entirely.
Standard RLHF fits a reward model to human preference comparisons using the Bradley-Terry model and a classification loss, then runs an RL stage that maximizes that reward while a KL term keeps the policy near a reference model, a three-phase pipeline that is complex and often unstable. [02738]
DPO's central move is that the KL-constrained reward-maximization problem solved in the RL stage has a closed-form solution: the KL divergence between a candidate policy πθ(y|x) and the distribution (1/Z(x))πref(y|x)exp((1/β)r(x,y)) is, by Gibbs' inequality, minimized at zero exactly when the two distributions coincide, so the optimal policy π* is that normalized, reward-tilted reference distribution. [00100]
Because that optimal-policy expression is intractable to use directly, since Z(x) requires summing over every possible string, it is instead rearranged to write the reward itself as r(x,y) = β log πr(y|x)/πref(y|x) + β log Z(x), turning a statement about rewards into an equivalent statement about a policy and a reference policy. [02738] [00100]
Substituting this reparameterized reward into the Bradley-Terry preference probability p*(y1≻y2|x) = σ(r*(x,y1) − r*(x,y2)) makes the intractable Z(x) cancel out of the difference, leaving human preference probability expressed purely through the optimal and reference policies, with no reward model in sight. [02738] [00100]
That yields a maximum-likelihood objective directly over the policy's own parameters, trained via ordinary supervised learning with a negative log-likelihood loss over an offline dataset of prompts paired with a preferred and dispreferred completion sampled from the reference policy. [02738] [00100]
The benefit is threefold: no reward model needs to be trained, no reinforcement learning loop is required, and the language model is optimized on human preferences using a well-understood supervised procedure instead of a notoriously fragile one. [00100]
Its documented weaknesses include a dependence on paired preference data that is not always easy to collect, sensitivity to label noise since it cannot account for the chance a preference was flipped, and an inability to sample fresh preference pairs from the current optimal policy because it never fits an explicit reward model. [00829]
These gaps motivated follow-on methods including KTO, which drops the need for paired data by maximizing a Kahneman-Tversky value function over individually labeled desirable and undesirable examples, RSO, which uses statistical rejection sampling to better approximate preference data from the target optimal policy, and IPO and conservative DPO, which add mechanisms that resist over-optimizing away from the reference model during long training runs. [00829]

Mixture-of-Experts architecture is the third advance covered here, and it decouples a model's total parameter count from the compute spent per token.
The intuition is conditional computation: instead of pushing every token through one dense feed-forward block, an MoE layer keeps n parallel expert feed-forward networks and a gating network that outputs a vector G(x) scoring each expert's relevance to the current token. [01053]
The layer's output is a weighted sum of the experts' outputs, each weighted by the corresponding entry of G(x), and a top-K gating rule restricts this sum to only the K highest-scoring experts by applying a softmax to the top-K logits of a linear layer rather than to all n, so K can be far smaller than n while the model still holds the full parameter space. [01053]
Mixtral 8x7B applies this by giving each transformer layer eight expert feed-forward blocks in place of one, routing every token to its top two experts, and as a result the model carries 47 billion total parameters but activates only about 13 billion of them to process any given token. [01053]
Because each expert can be assigned to a different accelerator through expert parallelism, sparse MoE layers fit naturally onto multi-GPU training and serving. [01053]
The open challenge that remains squarely on the training side is load balancing: ensuring an even distribution of tokens across experts is necessary to prevent bottlenecks and to make full use of the available compute, and it is flagged as a genuine engineering concern rather than a solved problem. [01053]

Substituting this reparameterized reward into the Bradley-Terry probability p(y1≻y2|x) = σ(r(x,y1) − r*(x,y2)) makes Z(x) cancel out of the difference, leaving preference probability expressed purely through the optimal and reference policies, with no reward model involved.

That yields a maximum-likelihood objective directly over the policy's parameters, trained by ordinary supervised learning with a negative log-likelihood loss over an offline dataset of prompts paired with preferred and dispreferred completions sampled from the reference policy.

The benefit is threefold: no reward model needs training, no reinforcement-learning loop is required, and the policy is optimized on preferences using a well-understood supervised procedure instead of a fragile one.

Its documented weaknesses include dependence on paired preference data that is not always easy to collect, sensitivity to label noise since it cannot account for a flipped preference, and an inability to sample fresh preference pairs from the current optimal policy because it never fits an explicit reward model.

These gaps motivated KTO, which drops paired data by maximizing a Kahneman-Tversky value function over individually labeled examples, RSO, which uses statistical rejection sampling to better approximate preference data from the target optimal policy, and IPO and conservative DPO, which resist over-optimizing away from the reference model during long training.
Mixture-of-Experts architecture is the third advance covered here, and it decouples a model's total parameter count from the compute spent per token.

The intuition is conditional computation: instead of pushing every token through one dense feed-forward block, an MoE layer keeps n parallel expert networks and a gating network outputting a vector G(x) scoring each expert's relevance to the current token.

The layer's output is a weighted sum of the experts' outputs weighted by G(x), and a top-K gating rule restricts this sum to the K highest-scoring experts by applying a softmax to only the top-K logits of a linear layer, so K can be far smaller than n while the model still holds the full parameter space.

Mixtral 8x7B applies this by giving each transformer layer eight expert blocks in place of one, routing every token to its top two experts, so the model carries 47 billion total parameters but activates only about 13 billion to process any given token.
Because each expert can be assigned to a different accelerator through expert parallelism, sparse MoE layers fit naturally onto multi-GPU training and serving.

The open challenge on the training side is load balancing: ensuring an even distribution of tokens across experts is necessary to prevent bottlenecks and make full use of available compute, and it remains flagged as a genuine engineering concern rather than a solved problem.
